name: Antanosi

catalog_citation: Ferrand, Gabriel. 1909. Essai de phonétique comparée du malais et des dialectes malgaches. Paris: Paul Geuthner. xlvii+347 pp. (thèse, Université de Paris). Open copy: archive.org item IA41547127_0068.
catalog_locator: Ch. VI 'L'accent tonique', pp. 236-237; Ch. III p. 164 for the Antanosi proparoxytons; cf. p. 201, p. 153, pp. 237-238 for suffix/compound rules, Introduction pp. XXXIX and XLVII (pp. 43, 51) for dialect identity.
catalog_quote: En Malgache, les thèmes radicaux quadrisyllabiques sont proparoxytons ou paroxytons: bakúraka, gros et mou, antsuhára, action de fortifier la poterie. Les thèmes radicaux trisyllabiques sont généralement proparoxytons, quelquefois paroxytons, très rarement oxytons: ánaka, enfant, atúdi, œuf, papakì, huître, húditra, peau, valála, sauterelle, kalaló, cancrelat, tánana, main, tanána, village. [p. 237] Les thèmes radicaux disyllabiques sont généralement paroxytons, très rarement oxytons: áti, foie, atí, ici, ári, rate, arí, là-bas, fénu, plein, umé, don. Tous les monossyllabes sont accentués: bé, grand, ló, pourri, tó, vrai, fí, délicieux. L'accent tonique des paroxytons et proparoxytons coïncide toujours avec l'accent temporel; en d'autres termes, toute voyelle initiale ou médiale accentuée est également longue [...] Ainsi que beaucoup d'autres langues, le malgache n'admet pas de finales longues. Comme conséquence de cette loi, les oxytons sont des thèmes à finale brève accentuée: papakì, umè, bè. [p. 164] L'ĕ sourd ou chuchoté est final, généralement en finale de proparoxyton où il répond à un ă Merina: Merina: lanitră, Antanosi: lanitsĕ, ciel, varutră, varutsĕ, commerce, efatră, efatsĕ, quatre, sambutră, sambutsĕ, prisonniers.
world_status: statement found in an open source

(p. 164)
new_statements.translation: In Malagasy, four-syllable roots are stressed on the antepenult or the penult [...] three-syllable roots are generally stressed on the antepenult, sometimes on the penult, very rarely on the final [...] two-syllable roots are generally stressed on the penult, very rarely on the final [...] All monosyllables are accented [...]. — Voiceless or whispered ĕ is final, generally as the final of an antepenult-stressed word, where it corresponds to Merina ă: Merina lanitră, Antanosy lanitsĕ 'sky'; varutră / varutsĕ 'trade'; efatră / efatsĕ 'four'; sambutră / sambutsĕ 'prisoners'.
new_statements.citation: Ferrand, Gabriel. 1909. Essai de phonétique comparée du malais et des dialectes malgaches. Paris: Paul Geuthner.
new_statements.locator: Ch. VI 'L'accent tonique', pp. 236-237 (pp. 296-297); with the Antanosi example set on p. 164 (p. 216); cf. p. 201 and p. 153
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: via its text 413 form-feed pages). (1) p. 296 (= p. 236, 'CHAPITRE VI / L'ACCENT TONIQUE'): 'En Malgache, les thèmes radicaux quadrisyllabiques sont proparoxytons ou [scanned: où] paroxytons : bakiraka.. antsuhara.. Les thèmes radicaux trisyllabiques sont généralement proparoxytons, quelquefois paroxytons, très rarement oxytons : anaka, huditra, tanana [hand] | atudi, valala, tanàna [village] | papakì, kalalé'. p. 297 (= p. 237): 'Les thèmes radicaux disyllabiques sont généralement paroxytons, très rarement oxytons.. Tous les monosyllabes sont accentués.. L'accent tonique des paroxytons et proparoxytons coïncide toujours avec l'accent temporel.. le malgache n'admet pas de fina…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Pan-Malagasy pattern, stated by Ferrand with his own Antanosy data: lexical accent on the penultimate syllable of the root/word by default; words ending in a weak (voiceless/whispered) final syllable — Merina -tra/-ka/-na, Tanosy -tse/-tsy, -ke/-ky — carry it on the antepenult (Ferrand's 'proparoxytons', explicitly exemplified for Antanosy); a small set of words are final-stressed (short accented final vowel: monosyllabic-root verbs, bé, umé, and SE-coastal apocopated nasal finals such as tanâ, lalàn where Merina has tanàna); suffixation shifts the accent one syllable to the right.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Ferrand: none described (all other root vowels short/atonic; compounds and reduplications keep the accent only on the last member, pp. 237-238). Howe 2017: 48-49 (general Malagasy) notes secondary stress on certain syllables before the primary in long words and on non-final members of compounds.
new_statements.exceptions: Oxytones with short accented final vowel (monosyllables and verbs built on them: là/mandà; bé, umé, papakì); SE/eastern dialects have disyllabic oxytones lalàn, tanàn / nasal-final tanâ, haravoâ = Merina paroxytone lalàna, tanàna (1909: 153; 1905 préface p. XIX-XX); quadrisyllabic roots vary between antepenult and penult; passive/imperative suffixes move the accent rightward, monosyllabic roots excepted.
new_statements.domain_note: Root / citation word ('thème radical'); accent described as lexical word accent coinciding with vowel length; morphological suffixation shifts it; not a phrase-level description. Ferrand's rule sentences are framed for Malagasy as a whole (Merina-based transcription with dialect forms); the Antanosy-specific content is the classification of Antanosy weak-final words as proparoxytons (p. 164, p. 201) and his statement that he recorded modern Antanosy himself (p. XLVII).
new_statements.identity_note: Ferrand's 'Antanosi (moderne)' = Tanosy of the Fort-Dauphin/Anosy coast (tano1246), which he says he recorded himself (1909: XLVII); his 'Antanosi ancien' = Flacourt's 1658 Fort-Dauphin dictionary (Old Tanosy). His placement rules (1909: 236-238) are framed for Malagasy generally (Merina-based forms plus dialect variants); only the proparoxyton/paroxyton classification of weak-final words is stated for Antanosy specifically (pp. 164, 201). The one dedicated modern description, Solo-Raharinjanahary 1984, concerns the Tanosy emigrant enclave on the Onilahy (Bezaha, SW Madagascar), not Fort-Dauphin. Howe 2017's general statement covers 'western and southwestern dialects' (-ke, -tse) and her sample includes Fort-Dauphin Tanosy speakers, but she gives no Tanosy-specific rule.

new_statements.quote: ACCENTUATION. La syllabe ou la lettre en italique doit être prononcée avec une pause et plus fortement que les autres. Exemple : manetrý se prononce ma-né-try en appuyant sur la syllabe né. ' — La syllabe ou la lettre portant ce signe doit être entièrement prononcée. Exemple : tendró se prononce tén-drou. ˘ — La syllabe ou la lettre portant ce signe doit être légèrement prononcée, la voyelle finale se faisant à peine entendre. Exemple : hazŏnă se prononce ha-z'-n'.
new_statements.translation: ACCENTUATION. The syllable or letter in italics must be pronounced with a pause and more strongly than the others. Example: manetrý is pronounced ma-né-try, leaning on the syllable né. ' — The syllable or letter bearing this sign must be pronounced in full. Example: tendró is pronounced tén-drou. ˘ — The syllable or letter bearing this sign must be pronounced lightly, the final vowel being barely heard. Example: hazŏnă is pronounced ha-z'-n'.
new_statements.citation: Jully, Antony. 1901. Manuel des dialectes malgaches. tanosy. Paris: J. André — page scan (archive.org item ManuelDesDialectesMalgaches).
new_statements.locator: Front matter, section 'Accentuation' on the unnumbered page [xxi] following p. xx (archive.org p. 26; djvu page index 25); Tanosy examples read from the vocabulary p. 1 'A' (p. 30) and p. 19 'C-D' (p. 48)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (125 pp., Google scan) via the saved render and low-res renders of pp. 25/26/30/48: p. 25 is the page numbered xx, p. 26 the unnumbered page with ABRÉVIATIONS / PRONONCIATION / DIPHTONGUES / ACCENTUATION, p. 30 = p. 1 'A', p. 48 = p. 19 'D' (running title MANUEL DES DIALECTES MALGACHES), so the locators hold. The ACCENTUATION passage on the page scan reads word for word as quoted, diacritics included ('manetrý se prononce ma-né-try en appuyant sur la syllabe né', 'tendró se prononce tén-drou', 'hazŏnă se prononce ha-z'-n''); the quote stops before two further notation lines (elision accent: renĭtantelў = rén'-tan-té-l'; ñ = gn), which is an acceptable excerpt; lines 2616-2627 hold th…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Ferrand 1909 statement (roots paroxytone; weak-final Antanosi words like lanitse, varutse, efatse proparoxytone): Jully's per-word italics put the stress on the penult of full-final Tanosy words and on the antepenult of -tse/-ke/-ne words. It adds nothing rule-shaped; its value is ~1,500 stress-marked Tanosy words from a 1900 Fort-Dauphin speaker, the earliest such marking for this dialect. The catalog_records entry for Antanosi has an empty rule field, so this work also supplies the missing rule wording indirectly.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Jully states no placement rule; he only explains his notation (italic = stressed syllable, acute = final fully pronounced, breve = final vowel barely heard) and then marks the stressed syllable in italics on every word of all seven dialect columns, Tanosy included (informant Idama of Fort-Dauphin, p. vii). Reading the Tanosy column from the page scan (pp. 1 and 19): stress on the penult in words with a full final vowel (manjetsý, mandavó, tendró, mipakă, hihakă, alokă, zakabé, lalekĕ, fitoké, mikaikĕ, mitsanó, mandreté, volý, hapohé) and on the antepenult in words ending in the reduced finals -tse/-ke/-ne/-tsy (miporatsĕ, holitsé, tsendrikĕ, fitsinjakĕ, fambolenĕ, atahoranĕ, manokitsy̆, tandrohotsy̆), i.e. penultimate stress counting the weak final as extrametrical — the same pattern Ferrand 1909 describes for Antanosi. The placement reading is derived from the word marks, not from a stated rule, and the italics were read from a Google scan at 300 dpi, so individual words may be misread.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated; in compounds two syllables are italicised (e.g. Tanosy manambelă helŏkă, sitrá sitranӑ), one per word.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The notation itself distinguishes full finals (acute: manjetsý, tendró, fitoké) from barely-heard finals (breve: lalekĕ, miporatsĕ, hihakă), the latter being the -tse/-ke words that carry antepenultimate marks.
new_statements.identity_note: Jully 1901 describes the Tanosy of Fort-Dauphin (informant Idama, province Antanosy, p. vii), i.e. the Anosy homeland variety, recorded in 1900 aboard ship and at the Paris Exposition; Ferrand 1909 (existing statement) covers modern Antanosi with Fort-Dauphin as principal village. Solo-Raharinjanahary 1984 is titled 'application à l'Antanosy' but was not opened.

sources.citation: Howe, Penelope. 2017. Tonogenesis in Central dialects of Malagasy: Acoustic and perceptual evidence with implications for synchronic mechanisms of sound change. PhD dissertation, Rice University.
sources.note: §2.3.6 p. 48 (general Malagasy, all dialects in her study incl. Tanosy speakers from Fort Dauphin): 'Most words have primary lexical stress on the penultimate syllable. However, lexical items ending in one of the weak final syllables (-na, -ka, -tra in Merina; -ke, -tse in western and southwestern dialects (Dahl 1952)..) have antepenultimate stress, and a small number of words have final-syllable stress'; secondary stress on certain pre-tonic syllables in long words. Tanosy word list Table C.10 p. 491 has no stress marks; no Tanosy-specific stress statement.

sources.citation: Ferrand, Gabriel. 1903. Essai de grammaire malgache. Paris: E. Leroux.
sources.note: §§97-103 (pp. 44-46): general Malagasy — disyllabic roots accented on the first syllable, trisyllabic on 1st or 2nd, quadrisyllabic on 2nd or 3rd; suffixation shifts accent; §60: Merina final -na corresponds to accented nasal final vowels in provincial dialects (tanâ, harië). Antanosy cited only for segmental/final correspondences (-tra ~ -tsa/-tse), not for accent.
Nothing on stress; lists Tanosy sound correspondences (-tra > -tsy, -ka > -ky, loss of final -na: vola, sofy) citing Catz & Catz; fr bibliography = Solo-Raharinjanahary 1984.

sources.note: Préface p. XVIII ff. 'Classification des voyelles des dialectes maritimes sud-orientaux' (the SE coastal dialects incl. Antanosy; Flacourt's 1658 dictionary is Old Tanosy of Fort-Dauphin): the long/tonic â 'peut être initial, proparoxyton, paroxyton, mais jamais oxyton'; short tonic vowels only final (monosyllables, verbs from monosyllabic roots, some imperatives); final nasal vowels 'toujours oxyton' (maivâ, tanâ, haravoâ) where Merina has paroxytone -âna (tanàna). No single placement rule sentence.
